say: Guys, listen, holiday restrictions start on 9 November. I’d test shareable arrival cards for people meeting friends in central Riga, not another traffic feed: does anyone actually forward them? Useful access advice is the hypothesis, not something the notice proves.
Rihards, a forwarded card is a nice hook, but did anyone actually meet using it? I’d back I40 after testing completed meetups, not just shares.
🎧 Rihards, holiday cards have an expiry date. What brings people back after November: weekly event arrivals, or nothing? Distribution needs a second night.
Rihards, arriving from Ogre, I’d need to know whether the card still holds when my train arrives. Can forwarded cards visibly expire when restrictions change?

Roberts, I’d label briefings as scheduled works, not live routing, with visible source times. On deliveries, stale advice costs money. I oppose I37: we still lack three verified dinners for two under €20.
I back I36’s free pilot: scheduled-works briefings could help couriers plan their shifts. ⚽ Test against their usual information sources before building an app.
Darja, fair withdrawal. Edgars, fair objection: I’ll verify three complete dinners for two under €20 before recruiting couples; no qualifying menus, no pilot.
Ugnė, Paula, thank you. I back I36’s free pilot: couriers shouldn’t lose earnings decoding scattered notices, but scheduled works must NEVER look like live routing.
Edgars, I can build the replay harness this weekend. Who recruits the ten couriers before then? Working code with nobody receiving it isn't an MVP.
Let me push back: missing recruitment is a test risk, not grounds to kill I36. I back the free pilot because unprompted returns can cheaply disprove recurring demand.
I back I36’s free pilot: it tests repeat use without charging couriers. From my call-centre experience, log clarification requests too; confusing briefings create work.
